what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Above the mechanics, an agent's policy is business logic
sections.para: The first agent rules are mechanical and vendors handle them well, but a few layers up a behaviour policy describes how the company works and what it is for. Much of that was never written down because software was the law, so it must now be written in layers, each with its own owner.

sections.label: The bottom is mechanics, and vendors do it well
sections.line: Mechanical controls are vendors' strength and need measuring
sections.para: The bottom layers are mechanical: the agent's own account, a platform-held token, delete switched off, outside forwarding blocked, sending needing a person. These are real boundaries. When the Google Workspace agent measured its connector on 19 September it found thirty tools, with send_message running unprompted while trashing needed approval.

sections.label: Above the mechanics is the business
sections.line: One layer up, the rules become the firm's business
sections.para: Above the mechanics sit function, process, relationship and organisation: reply in threads, never quote a price, invoice only after finance approval, nothing to a client in dispute except through legal, treat customers fairly. Each is a sentence a manager would say, and each layer has a different owner.

sections.label: Why the vendors stop at the mechanics
sections.line: Vendors build what is the same for every customer
sections.para: A control platform must scale, so it builds roles, switches, secret stores and approval prompts. The business layers differ per company, change weekly and are often unwritten. A vendor that models each customer becomes a consultancy, so the mechanical layer is a product and the business layers are the customer's to write.

sections.label: Software was the law
sections.line: Software enforced the rules nobody wrote down
sections.para: Companies never wrote their business logic down because their software was the law: no button to send an unapproved invoice, no screen showing payment details. An agent calls the API the button would have called, so a rule the interface enforced by omission is lost unless written in the behaviour policy and enforced.

sections.label: Policies inside policies
sections.line: Behaviour policies nest inside each other, layer by layer
sections.para: The structure that holds this is fractal: foundational controls, then soft controls, then function, process and relationship, with the company's purpose at the top. A policy describes rather than judges. It uses the same grammar as the site's fractal semantic graphs and the ABP's three-layer vocabulary.

sections.label: How much of it is hope?
sections.line: Of seventeen rules, five are controls and six hope
sections.para: Each rule is backed by a control, governed by an accepted risk, or resting on hope. In the example five of seventeen are controls, six accepted risks and six hope. The platform layer is all control, the organisation layer all hope, and the more firm-specific a rule, the more it rests on behaviour.

sections.label: Where the vendors plug in
sections.line: Vendors plug in by enforcing a written rule
sections.para: A vendor need only enforce the rules its product can reach: a send gateway, an outbound content check, a finance approval lookup, a legal blocked-recipients list each move a rule towards control. A control tied to a written rule shows what was bought, matching what RG.2 and AC.3 of the AI Baseline Control Framework ask.

sections.label: It looks a lot like a skill
sections.line: The upper layers read like a skill with controls
sections.para: A skill says how a function is done; a policy layer says what is allowed, who owns the rule and what stands in the way. Written together they codify the business for an agent, letting knowledge from a few heads and unreadable software be followed, reviewed and enforced, so the business can scale.

sections.label: What comes next
sections.line: Next, a real inbox counted before and after
sections.para: The fictional example comes next as a real one: the measured Gmail deployment as the bottom layers, upper layers written for one real inbox, the three states counted and published as a vault, then repeated with a vendor's control. Drafted from Dinis Cruz's voice note on 7 October 2026; no vendor was contacted.
